newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany deficit-plugging plan heads for rough ride.
newsitem.headline: Germany deficit-plugging plan heads for rough ride.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel won support on Thursday from conservative members of parliament for his controversial plan to plug gaping holes in the budget, but will have a hard time convincing anyone else of its merits.

With a huge tax shortfall hurting Germany's chances of qualifying for Europe's single currency, Waigel huddled in a two-hour emergency meeting with deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats and Christian Social Union.
The conservative deputies unananimously backed Waigel's plan to pick up the pace of selling government assets and tap Bundesbank reserves. He also wants to leave open the option of a tax increase.

But Kohl's coalition partners the Free Democrats ruled out tax increases and the opposition Social Democrats said Waigel was a failure and should resign. Waigel's plans to sell state holdings and revalue Bundesbank gold created a storm of protest.

The Bundesbank currently books its assets at their all-time lowest price or at the purchase price. A revaluation of the gold and currency reserves would deliver a windfall profit of up to 40 billion marks for Bonn, allowing it to retire old debt.

"I want to calm everyone by saying that not a single gram of gold, not a single ounce of gold and not a single dollar of currency reserves will be sold," Waigel said, straining to quell fears the government would raid the Bundesbank's holdings.

Ahead of an emergency session in parliament on Friday, newspaper editorials denounced Waigel for resorting to the "creative accounting" that he himself has so long scorned -- budget trickery that is sometimes used by European countries squirming to meet the Maastricht criteria on budget deficits.

Germany, once the star candidate for membership in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), is desperately trying to rein in its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product to make sure it qualifies for the euro's launch in 1999.
The talk of gold sales and asset revaluation follows the announcement on Wednesday that Bonn was considering an early sale of some of its Deutsche Telekom shares.
The Maastricht Treaty says countries joining EMU should have budget deficits no higher than three percent of gross domestic product and overall debts not more than 60 percent of GDP.

Several newspapers called Waigel's unprecedented grab for gold an act of desperation. They said it was a one-time budget accounting fudge that would neither help the economy nor solve any of the government's long term deficit problems.
"It could be that the emergency calculation makes arithmetic sense for this year, but it does not improve anything," wrote the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) daily.

"It shows the economic contortions that a country will manoeuvre itself into to be among the circle of nations that qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU), that what was once one of the most advanced and modern industrialised nations has to grab for the myth of a gold hoard."

The crisis erupted on Thursday when a tax commission reported the government's expected tax revenues for 1997 would fall 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) short of earlier targets, blowing a huge hole in Waigel's budget and diminishing Germany's chances of qualifying for the euro.
The commission said it also expected 1998 tax income for federal, state and local governments would be 31.6 billion marks below what Bonn had until now assumed.
Frankfurt bank analysts said they saw no chance for Germany to end this year at the three percent budget deficit target.
"He will have to eat his words and say that a number slightly above the three percent will be fine too," said Stefan Schneider of Paribas in the German financial capital.
